KEY MESSAGE 1...A powerful coastal storm is expected to bring 
severe impacts to the region due to damaging high winds 
starting late tonight, peaking during Thanksgiving Day, and 
departing into Friday.

Confidence is high that a powerful coastal storm will bring
severe impacts to the area on Thanksgiving Day. The storm will 
begin to develop offshore of the Carolina coast today.

Synoptics:

A strong upper-low will shift eastward out of the central US, 
with strong divergence aloft favoring surface cyclogenesis just 
off the southeast coast. From there, the low is expected to 
track northward while remaining inland towards the Mid Atlantic
through Thursday. Guidance remains quite consistent on the 
development and rapid deepening of this low, and remains mostly
in good agreement as far as timing and the storm track. The 
GFS, RGEM, and ECMWF all track the low northward from the coast 
of the Carolinas northward towards western PA.

A ~1044 mb high will be in place near the Gulf of Maine tonight,
which will shift eastward toward Nova Scotia into Thursday. 
Meanwhile, the ~995 mb surface low, which has trended slightly 
stronger and further west, will race northward into Thursday. 
This will create a very strong pressure gradient across our 
region, with surface pressure falls of near 35 mb in 24 hours 
(greater than 1 mb/hour) locally. A powerful low level jet is 
forecast to develop in response ahead of the low and sweep 
northward along the coast, with 925 mb winds in the 70-85 kts 
range. Notably, the 925 mb level is below the marine layer 
inversion, however the mixed boundary layer will be shallower 
than this (~1000 feet deep or so). Even then, GFS BUFKIT 
profiles indicate winds speeds within the mixed layer in the 
50-60 kts range across the coastal plain of NJ and Delmarva, and
in the 45-55 kts range as far inland as the Philly metro,
southeastern PA, and portions of northern NJ. Due to the
dynamics and thermodynamics of this storm, we anticipate these
boundary layer winds to mix down to the surface in the form of
widespread, frequent wind gusts of 50-70 mph, strongest near the
coast and across Delmarva.


Impacts:

We now have high confidence in specific impacts across much of
the area.

Winds: The most severe impact from this storm aside from coastal
flooding (see separate coastal flooding key message below) will
be from damaging high winds. Northeast to east winds will begin
ramping up late tonight before peaking Thursday. Gusts of 50 to
70 mph are likely across our entire area, including inland. The
strongest winds are expected to occur along the coast and inland
across the coastal plain of Delmarva and southern NJ. Gusts
could potentially exceed 70 mph during heavy rainbands along 
the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware. Sustained winds 
along the immediate coast will be near 35-45 mph, potentially 
briefly stronger during heavy rainbands. A High Wind Warning is
now in effect for almost all of our area, where confidence is 
high in wind gusts reaching 60-70 mph. A Wind Advisory is in 
effect for Sussex and Morris Counties in NJ for wind gusts in 
the 45-55 mph range, although wind gusts may reach 60 mph along 
ridge lines and mountain peaks in this area. The Warnings and 
Advisories are in effect starting late tonight through Thursday 
evening. Widespread tree damage and power outages are likely 
across much of our area during Thanksgiving Day, especially 
toward the coast and across Delmarva. The winds are expected to 
subside overnight Thursday night, however some guidance suggests
southwest to west winds will increase with gusts near 35 to 45 
mph possible again Friday afternoon and evening.

Rain: Given recent dryness and the progressive nature of this 
system, freshwater flooding does not appear to be as significant
of a concern, but this threat will continue to be monitored as 
rainfall amounts come into better focus. A general 1-3" of rain
is forecast, with the greatest amounts toward the coast. The 
Weather Prediction Center has the area in a MARGINAL Risk for 
excessive rainfall, and a SLIGHT Risk was introduced for coastal
areas. Any flooding impacts should be confined mainly to urban 
flooding and flooding of low lying, poor drainage areas, as well
as some of our more sensitive streams and creeks. The heaviest
rainfall amounts will occur in areas that are forecast to
receive significant coastal flooding with Coastal Flood Warnings
in effect, and thus no fresh water flood products would be 
issued in conjunction with these. The heavy rainfall could 
exacerbate coastal flooding issues though. Some light rain may 
linger on Friday, especially northwest of I-95, but any rainfall
on Friday will be inconsequential.
